newsitem.title: USA: NYC Democratic mayoral hopefuls debate.
newsitem.headline: NYC Democratic mayoral hopefuls debate.

text.p: New York City's Democratic mayoral hopefuls gathered Wednesday for the campaign's first debate, ganging up to accuse Mayor Rudolph Giuliani of policies that harm minorities, the poor, the elderly and the young.

Manhattan Borough President Ruth Messinger, Bronx Borough President Fernando Ferrer, Brooklyn City Councilman Sal Albanese and the Rev. Al Sharpton are vying to win the Sept. 10 Democratic primary and challenge Giuliani in the November general election. But the Republican incumbent is way ahead in opinion polls.

Displaying a friendly and often united front, the four denounced Giuliani on such issues as budget cuts in education, a subway fare hike and programmes they say do not provide useful training or job opportunities for people moving off welfare.

"Giuliani's problem is not that he's Republican. His problem is he's repugnant," said Sharpton, an outspoken activist minister and the only black mayoral candidate. "Rudy Giuliani is the mayor of part of the city," he said. "I'm running because we need a mayor to service the entire city."

Ferrer, the only Hispanic candidate, emphasised his track record overseeing a rebuilding of the city's Bronx borough, once a grim picture of urban crime and decay. He touted its new housing, job creation and improved access to health care, saying "I have overseen what everyone agrees is a miracle."

Albanese mourned the passing of economic opportunities such as those his family enjoyed when they immigrated from Italy. "We're rapidly moving toward a two-tier city of a few very wealthy people and the rest of the city poor and working poor," he said.

Messinger criticised the mayor for listening too closely to special interests. "He has ignored the needs of New York to follow his own whims and the wishes of a powerful few," she said, referring to a proposed $1 billion New York Yankees baseball stadium in midtown Manhattan.

Giuliani, a former federal prosecutor known for a tough, no-nonsense approach to running the city, defeated David Dinkins, the city's first black mayor, in 1993. Polls show voters largely satisfied with life under the Giuliani administration, especially a drop in crime rates to their lowest levels in a generation.
Each of the Democrats in the debate said they would support the winner of the party's primary in the general election.
